newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Significant downside risks for NZ economy - ANZ.
newsitem.headline: Significant downside risks for NZ economy - ANZ.

text.p: ANZ Bank economists said on Friday they saw the New Zealand economy as vulnerable to a slowdown if business and investor confidence slides.

"The downside risks for the economy are significant, even over the near term, and we remain concerned that business and consumer confidence could easily be dented," the economists said in the latest edition of ANZ's Economic Focus.
ANZ still expects GDP to grow by about two percent in 1997 and three percent in 1998.

However, easier fiscal policy would need to be compensated by tighter than otherwise monetary policy. This meant that government and household consumption would account for a higher proportion of growth, while exports and business investment would be constrained.
"Economic growth will therefore be less balanced and less sustainable, raising the risks of a sharper slowdown in the economy some time in the future," ANZ said.
The economy was in a "precarious" state and if confidence was significantly dented, a more protracted slowdown was very likely.

ANZ said it expected construction activity to moderate in 1997 after a very robust spell of growth. Retailing would be constrained by the slowdown in employment and wages growth, and rising household debt was also likely to curb spending.
Exporters would continue to suffer the lagged effects of a soft global economy and a loss of price competitiveness due to the strength of the currency.
"Barring a significant decline in the NZ dollar, it is hard to spy the origins of a substantial recovery in exports."

ANZ said the impetus to the economy from an extra $5 billion of government spending over three years may be cancelled out if the associated inflationary risk pushed up short-term interest rates and the New Zealand dollar.
ANZ said most of the easing in monetary conditions that began in mid-December had taken the form of lower interest rates rather than a significant drop in the currency.

"This is unlikely to bring much relief to the export sector, while the risk that lower interest rates might stimulate renewed demand in the housing market remains a potential threat to the inflation outlook," ANZ said.

Prospects for lower inflation were good, although falls in interest rates were likely to be more modest than in recent months. The Reserve Bank would remain mindful of the longer term risks to inflation, which could cause it to tighten monetary policy from late 1997.
ANZ expects firmer world interest rates during 1997, and said this would help make New Zealand rates relatively less attractive to foreign investors.
"That, in turn, will help to reduce the upward pressure on the NZ dollar evident during 1996," the economists said.
